Now, there are actually quite a few barriers to the development of workers' co-ops, and their supposed 'lack of greater efficiency' as compared to other forms of enterprise in some ideal abstract 'level playing ground' isn't one of them. One of the first recognized and much discussed is the initial lack of capital on the part of the average worker. This was a problem that was heavily looked at in the early labor movement in France by unionists who described themselves as 'mutualists'.

Here's how it works. Set up a game with supposedly equal odds of winning with two players. Let player 1 begin with five dollars and player 2 begin with $10,000. Begin the game with an equal $1 bet for both parties, but there is no limit to how much you can bet. Player two will always clean out player one in any realistic tournament. The optimal strategy for player two is to bet all of the money held by player one. In order for player one to have even the ghost of a chance the odds (efficiency) have to be massively in his favor. Work out the mathematics if you like. You'll find that simply being say 3 to 4 Xs (efficient) just won't cut it. In other words if a worker controlled enterprise is 400% more 'efficient' in this sort of situation it still can't compete on the mythical 'level playing field'.
